2.text: Kereˊtkun desires to accept the sacrifice: therefore it is kept up all the time,

3.text: from early in the morning until late in the evening. Small chips of wood,

4.text: bones, and blubber, serve for fuel. The Asiatic Eskimo substitute for the

5.text: fire another big lamp; or they sacrifice to Kereˊtkun on the lamp where he

6.text: has taken his place. This difference is significant, as the lamp in the place

7.text: of the hearth, is better adapted to the woodless tundra and to arctic mari-

8.text: time life than the hearth of the Chukchee ceremonial.

9.text: Quantities of pudding made of edible roots and stalks mixed with oil

10.text: and liver are considered necessary for the ceremonial. We find the same

11.text: feature in the ceremonies of the Reindeer Chukchee, the Koryak, and, formerly,

12.text: in those ot the Kamchadal, who declared that Kutq was exceedingly fond of

14.text: Families of friends and relatives take part in preparing the necessary

15.text: pudding, and their women come every morning to the house where the cele-

16.text: bration is going on, bringing a new supply. The guests gather a little later,

17.text: and each woman brings a vessel in which she receives part to take home.

18.text: Besides the pudding, all kinds of food are distributed in profusion to those

19.text: assembled, and considerable time is used in eating and in drinking tea.

20.text: The first day of the ceremonial is considered as belonging to the inmates

21.text: of the house, who beat the drum, sing their tunes, and prepare ceremonial

22.text: dances in a way similar to that of the Reindeer Chukchee. The drummers

23.text: are men, who stand in the usual place, — on the outer side of the hearth,

24.text: facing the sleeping-room. The dancers, who are women, stand on the inner

25.text: side of the hearth, facing the entrance. All the participants are singing, each

26.text: his own tune. Some of the people have small whistles of wood or goose-

27.text: quill, by means of which, from time to time, they send forth a short, shrill

28.text: sound (see Fig. 281). This is done mainly by the children of the family,

29.text: who have to skip around the hearth.

30.text: The second day belongs to the guests, and particularly to the shamans,

31.text: who have to show, in turn, their skill in drumming and singing.

32.text: The third day belongs to the women, who act both as drummers and

33.text: dancers. The drummers stand in the usual place of the men, — on the outer

34.text: side of the hearth, facing the sleeping-room; and the dancers, in the usual

35.text: place of the women, — on the inner side of the hearth, facing the entrance.

36.text: All this is similar, even in the minor details, to the customs of the Rein-

37.text: deer people in the fall ceremonial and the “thanksgiving.” A new detail is

38.text: that of a night-watch, which must be kept for the sake of Kereˊtkun, who

39.text: is supposed to stay in the house all the time. This watch is kept by an

40.text: old man or woman. A shaman is often invited especially for this purpose,

41.text: and at the end of the watch he receives a coil of new thong in pay for

42.text: his services. During his watch he sits on a whale’s vertebra which is used
